chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. Equal sharing gives the fractional unit, measuring and the number line make a fraction a length and a number, and one idea, write both fractions in the same fractional unit, carries comparing, adding and subtracting.

points.title: Shares before symbols
points.text: Every new idea starts from a share of roti, chikki or a paper strip, so the symbol 3/4 always means three pieces of one quarter.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, one tool to do it by hand, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.

points.title: One unit for everything
points.text: Equivalent fractions are the tool: to compare, add or subtract, rewrite both fractions in the same fractional unit, then count units.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as '1/9 is more than 1/5' or '1/2 + 1/3 makes 2/5', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a picture, never just a rule.

concepts.concept_name: Halves and quarters of a roti

content.text:
Recall that when some whole number of things are shared equally among some number of people, fractions tell us how much each share is.
Shabnam: Do you remember, if one roti is divided equally between two children, how much roti will each child get?
Mukta: Each child will get half a roti.
Shabnam: The fraction 'one half' is written as 1/2. We also sometimes read this as 'one upon two.'
Mukta: If one roti is equally shared among 4 children, how much roti will one child get?
Shabnam: Each child's share is 1/4 roti.
Mukta: And which is more 1/2 roti or 1/4 roti?
Shabnam: When 2 children share 1 roti equally, each child gets 1/2 roti. When 4 children share 1 roti equally, each child gets 1/4 roti. Since, in the second group more children share the same one roti, each child gets a smaller share. So, 1/2 roti is more than 1/4 roti.

concepts.concept_name: Fractional units: more sharers, smaller share

content.text:
Beni: Which fraction is greater: 1/5 or 1/9?
Arvin: 9 is bigger than 5. So I would guess that 1/9 is greater than 1/5. Am I right?
Beni: No! That is a common mistake. Think of these fractions as shares.
Arvin: If one roti is shared among 5 children, each one gets a share of 1/5 roti. If one roti is shared among 9 children, each one gets a share of 1/9 roti?
Beni: Exactly! Now think again, which share is higher?
Arvin: If I share with more people, I will get less. So, 1/9 < 1/5.
Beni: You got it!
Oh, so 1/100 is bigger than 1/200!
When one unit is divided into several equal parts, each part is called a fractional unit. These are all fractional units: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, ..., 1/10, ..., 1/50, ..., 1/100, etc.
We also sometimes refer to fractional units as 'unit fractions.'
Fractions have been used and named in India since ancient times. In the Rig Veda, the fraction 3/4 is referred to as tri-pada. This has the same meaning as the words for 3/4 in many Indian languages today, e.g., 'teen paav' in colloquial Hindi and 'mukkaal' in Tamil. Indeed, words for fractions used today in many Indian languages go back to ancient times.
Find out and discuss the words for fractions that are used in the different languages spoken in your home, city, or state. 1. Think of 1/5 as the share each child gets when 1 roti is shared among 5 children.
2. 1/9 is the share when 1 roti is shared among 9 children.

4. So 1/9 < 1/5, which means 1/5 is greater. In the same way 1/100 is bigger than 1/200.

steps: Ask family members and classmates for their words for 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1 1/4, 1 1/2 and 2 1/2.
Write each word next to the fraction it means.
Compare the words across languages.
content.answer: Answers vary. For example, in colloquial Hindi: half = aadha, quarter = paav, three quarters = teen paav, one and a quarter = savaa, one and a half = dedh, two and a half = dhaai. In Tamil, three quarters = mukkaal.

content.text:

Several shares of 1/n are counted: 3 × 1/4 = 3/4.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q5 (section 7.1)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q5 (section 7.1): Arrange these fraction words in order of size from the smallest to the biggest: One and a half, three quarters, one and a quarter, half, quarter, two and a half.
1. Write each word as a fraction: quarter = 1/4, half = 1/2, three quarters = 3/4, one and a quarter = 1 1/4, one and a half = 1 1/2, two and a half = 2 1/2.
2. Those less than 1: 1/4 < 1/2 < 3/4 (1 quarter, 2 quarters, 3 quarters).
3. Those between 1 and 2: 1 1/4 < 1 1/2, since a quarter is less than a half.
4. 2 1/2 is the biggest because it has 2 wholes.
Answer: quarter (1/4), half (1/2), three quarters (3/4), one and a quarter (1 1/4), one and a half (1 1/2), two and a half (2 1/2)

content.text:
Worked example: A whole chikki is a rectangle made of 24 equal small squares (6 across, 4 down). It is broken into 2 pieces: a small rectangle 3 squares across and 2 squares down, and the remaining bigger L-shaped piece. How much of the original chikki is each piece?
1. Cutting the chikki in half both ways makes 4 equal pieces of 3 by 2 squares, so the small piece is 1/4.
2. The bigger piece holds 3 pieces of size 1/4.
3. 3 × 1/4 = 3/4, so the bigger piece is 3/4 chikki.
Answer: Small piece 1/4 chikki; bigger piece 3/4 chikki.

concepts.concept_name: Measuring a chikki piece in quarters

content.text:
Worked example: A whole chikki (24 equal small squares, 6 across and 4 down) is divided into 6 equal parts in two different ways: once into 6 rectangles (each 2 squares by 2 squares) and once with slanted cuts into 6 pieces including triangles. We get 1/6 chikki pieces of different shapes. Are they of the same size?
1. The whole chikki is 24 small squares.
2. 6 equal parts of 24 squares means each part is 24 ÷ 6 = 4 squares.
3. The rectangle piece and the triangle piece both cover 4 squares' worth, so both are 1/6 and have the same size.
Answer: Yes, they are of the same size. Each is 1/6 of the chikki (4 small squares' worth), only the shapes differ.

content.text:
Figure it Out (section 7.2): The pieces below are different fractional units of a whole chikki. The whole chikki is a rectangle of 24 equal small squares (6 across, 4 down). How much of a whole chikki is each piece? a) A rectangle 1 square across and 2 squares down. b) A right triangle with legs 4 squares tall and 3 squares wide (half of a 3 by 4 block). c) A right triangle with legs 2 squares tall and 3 squares wide (half of a 3 by 2 block). d) A strip 1 square across and 4 squares down. e) An L-shape made of 3 squares. f) A triangle with a vertical side 4 squares long and its tip 2 squares to the right (half of a 2 by 4 block). g) A single small square. h) A right triangle with legs 2 squares tall and 1 square wide (half of a 1 by 2 block).
1. The whole chikki has 6 × 4 = 24 small squares.
2. Count the squares in each piece (a triangle is half of its rectangle): a 2, b 6, c 3, d 4, e 3, f 4, g 1, h 1.
3. Find how many such pieces make the whole: 24 ÷ 2 = 12, 24 ÷ 6 = 4, 24 ÷ 3 = 8, 24 ÷ 4 = 6, 24 ÷ 1 = 24.
4. So the pieces are 1/12, 1/4, 1/8, 1/6, 1/8, 1/6, 1/24, 1/24.
Answer: a) 1/12, b) 1/4, c) 1/8, d) 1/6, e) 1/8, f) 1/6, g) 1/24, h) 1/24

content.text:
Take a strip of paper. We consider this paper strip to be one unit long.
Fold the strip into two equal parts and then open up the strip again. Taking the strip to be one unit in length, what are the lengths of the two new parts of the strip created by the crease?
What will you get if you fold the previously-folded strip again into two equal parts? You will now get four equal parts.
1/4; 2 × 1/4 = 2/4; 3 × 1/4 = 3/4; 4 × 1/4 = 4/4
Do it once more! Fill in the blank boxes.
8 × 1/8 = 8/8 = 1
Fractional quantities can be measured using fractional units.

content.text:
Worked example: What will you get if you fold the already half-folded paper strip again into two equal parts? Name the lengths of 1, 2, 3 and 4 of the new parts.
1. Each half is folded into 2, so the strip has 2 × 2 = 4 equal parts.
2. Each part is 1/4 unit.
3. Counting parts: 2 × 1/4 = 2/4, 3 × 1/4 = 3/4, 4 × 1/4 = 4/4, which is the whole strip.
Answer: Four equal parts, each 1/4 unit: 1/4, 2 × 1/4 = 2/4, 3 × 1/4 = 3/4, 4 × 1/4 = 4/4.

concepts.concept_name: Collecting halves, and reading fractions

content.text:
Let us look at another example,
1/2 = 1 × 1/2; 1/2 + 1/2 = 2 × 1/2; 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 3 × 1/2; 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 4 × 1/2; 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 5 × 1/2
We can describe how much the quantity is by collecting together the fractional units.
We usually read the fraction 3/4 as 'three quarters' or 'three upon four', but reading it as '3 × 1/4' helps us to understand the size of the fraction because it clearly shows what the fractional unit is (1/4) and how many such fractional units (3) there are.
Recall what we call the top number and the bottom number of fractions. In the fraction 5/6, 5 is the numerator and 6 is the denominator.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (section 7.3)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 7.3): The table of 1/2 goes: 1/2 = 1 × 1/2, 1/2 + 1/2 = 2 × 1/2, and so on up to 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 5 × 1/2. Continue this table of 1/2 for 2 more steps.
1. The last row has 5 halves.
2. Add one more 1/2: six 1/2 added = 6 × 1/2 (that is 3 full rotis).
3. Add one more 1/2: seven 1/2 added = 7 × 1/2 (3 full rotis and a half).

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 7.3): Can you create a similar table for 1/4 (like the table of half rotis)?
1. The fractional unit is a quarter roti, 1/4.
2. Each new row adds one more 1/4.
3. 4 quarters make 1 full roti: 4 × 1/4 = 4/4 = 1.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (section 7.3): Make 1/3 using a paper strip. Can you use this to also make 1/6?
1. Fold the 1 unit strip into 3 equal parts: each part is 1/3.
2. Fold the folded strip into 2 equal parts: each third is cut into 2.
3. Now there are 3 × 2 = 6 equal parts, so each part is 1/6.
Answer: Yes. Fold the strip into 3 equal parts to get 1/3; then fold it in half so each third splits into 2, giving 6 equal parts, each 1/6.

Hop that many gaps from 0, counting past 1 if needed.

media.description: A blue line runs from zero to the first mark on a number line where the distance from zero to one is cut into two equal parts. The board finds the size of one part, counts the parts under the blue line and checks that two parts fill one unit. Keeko doubts the answer by reading the first mark as the number one.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: cut one unit into equal parts, then count the parts a line covers to read its length. Watch for students who read the first mark as one instead of counting parts.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.
